# Vāseṭṭha Sutta (MN 98 (PTS MN ii 196))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Vāseṭṭha Sutta* (MN 98; PTS MN ii 196) depicts the Buddha resolving a dispute between two young Vedic scholars, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, regarding what constitutes a true brahmin: birth (*jāti*) or ethical deeds (*kamma*) [SuttaCentral; Collins 1993; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha answers with a biological classification (*jātivibhaṅga*): whereas distinct biological species and markers exist throughout the plant and animal kingdoms (distinguishing four-footed beasts, reptiles, birds, and fish), no such inherent biological differences exist among human beings [SuttaCentral; Rahula 1956; Collins 1993]. The discourse argues that caste and social status are merely nominal, conventional designations; a person's standing is determined solely by moral conduct and spiritual attainment, with the true brahmin redefined as the *arahant* [Rahula 1956; Obeyesekere; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Davis and Flanagan]. At the conclusion, the stanzas culminate with the refrain "him I call a brahmin," and the interlocutors declare themselves lay followers [Collins 1993; Obeyesekere].
Unusually within the canon, the discourse is preserved identically in both the *Majjhimanikāya* (MN 98) and the *Sutta Nipāta* (Snp 3.9) [Rahula 1956; Winternitz 1933; McTighe]. Because the text duplicates Snp 3.9, the original Pali Text Society edition of the *Majjhimanikāya* edited by Trenckner and Chalmers omitted the full text, referring readers instead to the PTS edition of the *Sutta Nipāta* [McTighe; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Modern scholars have discussed this duplication in the context of the relative chronology and borrowing between the *Suttanipāta* and the *Majjhimanikāya* [Winternitz 1933].
The closing verse cycle of MN 98 corresponds closely to the Brāhmaṇavagga of the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 386, 396–423) [SuttaCentral; Obeyesekere]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus confirms extensive Pali-internal sharing with Snp 3.9 (8,946 characters) and Dhp (7,802 characters), as well as formulaic links with the *Tevijja Sutta* (DN 13), which features the same protagonists [Collins 1993; DharmaNexus]. Beyond Pali, SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus identify parallels to the verse sections in the *Gāndhārī Dharmapada* (1–50), the *Patna Dharmapada* (34–49), the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* (chapter 33), and Chinese translations (T 210, T 212, T 213) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
